ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Regional Ethics Committee of Friuli Venezia Giulia and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Thirty-eight autistic participants were compared with a large neurotypical sample for personality and with neurotypical individuals selected with high (HA) or low (LA) agreeableness during three EEG paradigms examining social-interaction perception, basic emotion recognition, and complex mental-state decoding.
Second, we asked whether autistic participants were more similar in agreeableness to neurotypical individuals with relatively low rather than high agreeableness.
table.header: Social cognition represents a particularly relevant domain in which to examine this variability.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Autism spectrum disorder is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in social-cognitive functioning, yet individual differences contributing to this variability remain poorly understood.
Personality provides a normative framework for characterizing such differences across diagnostic boundaries.

Here, we investigated whether personality, particularly agreeableness, relates to behavioral and neural variability in social cognition in autistic young adults without intellectual and language impairment.

Thirty-eight autistic participants were compared with a large neurotypical sample for personality and with neurotypical individuals selected with high (HA) or low (LA) agreeableness during three EEG paradigms examining social-interaction perception, basic emotion recognition, and complex mental-state decoding.
Autistic participants showed lower agreeableness, extraversion, and conscientiousness and higher neuroticism than neurotypical participants, with substantial interindividual variability.
Their agreeableness scores were closer to those of LA than HA participants.

Behavioral differences were selective: autistic participants showed lower accuracy than HA participants during complex mental-state decoding, whereas no significant difference was detected relative to LA participants or during the other social-cognitive tasks.
Neural activity revealed a more nuanced pattern.
No significant group differences emerged during social-interaction perception or basic emotion recognition.
In contrast, decoding of complex mental states from the face revealed group differences in the ERP component N170 and a smaller Late Slow Wave (LSW) response in autistic participants.
The LSW difference was more extensive relative to HA than to LA neurotypical participants.
Overall, these findings highlight the importance of considering individual variability at both behavioral and neural levels, as similar behavioral outcomes may reflect distinct neural processing.

Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a clinical label encompassing substantial variability in social, cognitive, linguistic, and adaptive functioning (Lai et al., 2013; Lord et al., 2020; Warrier et al., 2018).

text.text: With the introduction of the DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), previous diagnostic categories, including autistic disorder, Asperger syndrome, and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified, were merged into a single spectrum.
While this conceptualization acknowledges the heterogeneous and dimensional nature of autism, it also brings together individuals with considerably different profiles.

Such heterogeneity represents a major challenge for understanding the neurobiological and cognitive variability associated with autism and may partly account for the inconsistent findings reported across studies (Bertelsen et al., 2021; Mottron, 2020; Vincent et al., 2020).

text.text: Recent research has therefore emphasized the importance of considering individual variability alongside group-level differences in autism (Wang, 2022; Floris et al., 2025).

text.text: This issue is especially relevant when considering autistic adults without intellectual disability and with preserved language abilities (a group that, before DSM-5, often received a diagnosis of Asperger syndrome).

Intellectual and language abilities alone may not adequately capture their social-cognitive and adaptive profiles, and individuals who are relatively independent in some areas of everyday functioning may nevertheless have specific needs that become particularly relevant in adulthood (Kamp-Becker et al., 2010; Liss et al., 2001; Renty et al., 2006).

text.text: Research on autistic adults without intellectual disability also indicates that available post-diagnostic services do not always correspond to the support they report as useful, further highlighting the importance of considering variability within this population rather than assuming that relatively preserved intellectual and language abilities correspond to homogeneous functioning or support needs (Norris et al., 2025).

text.text: Characterizing factors that contribute to individual variability within this group may therefore provide information that is not captured by the diagnostic label alone.
Theory of Mind (ToM), broadly defined as the ability to represent and understand others' mental states, plays a central role in social interactions (Frith & Frith, 2010; Schurz et al., 2014).

text.text: However, social cognition is not a unitary process and cannot be adequately characterized by a single measure.
It comprises partially dissociable processes, including social perception, emotion recognition, and mentalizing, which differ in the type and complexity of information that needs to be processed.
Recent work has further emphasized the multifaceted nature of social cognition in autism, including differences across its components and between explicit and implicit processing (Bölte, 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work has further emphasized the multifaceted nature of social cognition in autism, including differences across its components and between explicit and implicit processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bölte, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A more informative approach may therefore be to determine which components of social cognition vary across autistic individuals, at which stages of processing this variability emerges, and which individual characteristics contribute to it.
One potential source of this individual variability is personality.

The Five-Factor Model (FFM; Costa & McCrae, 1992; Goldberg, 1990) describes personality along five continuous dimensions (i.e., extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness) which capture individual differences in emotional, motivational, cognitive, and behavioral tendencies.

text.text: The role of personality and individual differences in autism has received considerably less attention than core diagnostic features.

Previous studies have reported, on average, lower extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, openness and emotional stability in autistic individuals, although the magnitude and consistency of these differences vary across studies (Austin, 2005; Kanai et al., 2011; Lodi-Smith et al., 2019; Schwartzman et al., 2016; Strunz et al., 2015; Wakabayashi et al., 2006).

text.text: Personality traits have also been associated with individual differences in internalizing and externalizing behaviors in autistic children and with the quality of life and the adaptive outcomes in autistic adults (De Pauw et al., 2011; Ratner & Burrow, 2017; Rodgers et al., 2018; Schriber et al., 2014; Schwartzman et al., 2016).

text.text: Importantly, however, average group differences do not imply the existence of a uniform personality profile associated with autism.

The variable effect sizes reported in previous studies and the substantial variability across samples suggest instead that broad personality dimensions may provide a complementary way of characterizing individual differences within the spectrum (Lodi-Smith et al., 2019; Schwartzman et al., 2016).

text.text: Interpretation of the existing literature is further complicated by the heterogeneity of the samples considered.

Personality studies have included participants differing considerably in age, intellectual and language abilities, and clinical characteristics, and have mainly relied on self-or other-report measures (Lodi-Smith et al., 2019; Robinson et al., 2020; Schwartzman et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Personality studies have included participants differing considerably in age, intellectual and language abilities, and clinical characteristics, and have mainly relied on self-or other-report measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lodi-Smith et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Robinson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Schwartzman et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, whether personality differences are also associated with differences in the processing of social information in autistic adults remains largely unexplored.

This question is particularly relevant in individuals without intellectual disability and with preserved language abilities, for whom performance in explicit behavioral tasks may not fully characterize the processes through which social information is analyzed.
Electrophysiological measures can complement behavioral performance by providing information about the temporal dynamics of these processes.

Previous EEG studies in autism have indeed reported differences in the timing and pattern of neural responses to social and emotional information compared with neurotypical individuals, particularly during face perception and the processing of socially relevant information (e.g., Benning et al., 2016; Fan et al., 2014; Hileman et al., 2011; Kang et al., 2018; Lerner et al., 2013).

text.text: Together, these findings highlight the value of examining neural differences between autistic and neurotypical individuals across different stages of social-cognitive processing, while also considering how individual characteristics may contribute to the observed patterns.
Among the five personality dimensions, agreeableness is particularly relevant to social cognition.

Agreeableness reflects individual differences in prosocial tendencies, cooperation, empathy, and interpersonal sympathy (Costa & McCrae, 1992; Goldberg, 1990), and has been associated with social cognition and ToM abilities (Allen & DeYoung, 2017; DeYoung & Blain, 2020; Nettle & Liddle, 2008; Udochi et al., 2022).

text.text: Our previous studies on neurotypical individuals showed that individual differences in agreeableness are associated with how social and emotional information is processed at both behavioral and neural levels.

Using fMRI, we found that individuals with higher agreeableness showed a greater differentiation between neural representations of social and non-social information in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, a region consistently involved in mentalizing (Arbula et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Using fMRI, we found that individuals with higher agreeableness showed a greater differentiation between neural representations of social and non-social information in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, a region consistently involved in mentalizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arbula et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We subsequently used EEG to investigate when during social information processing the influence of agreeableness emerges.

During the perception of social interactions, higher agreeableness was associated with a greater neural differentiation between social and non-social scenes, with effects emerging at relatively early stages of processing (Pisanu et al., 2024a).
text.formatted: During the perception of social interactions, higher agreeableness was associated with a greater neural differentiation between social and non-social scenes, with effects emerging at relatively early stages of processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Pisanu et al., 2024a)</ref>.

text.text: In another study, we examined emotional information processing at different levels of complexity by comparing the recognition of basic emotions conveyed by biological motion with the decoding of complex mental states from the eye region.

Agreeableness modulated neural responses during complex mental-state decoding, but not during the recognition of basic emotional actions, with the effect emerging in a late time window, and source estimates pointing to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Pisanu et al., 2024b).
text.formatted: Agreeableness modulated neural responses during complex mental-state decoding, but not during the recognition of basic emotional actions, with the effect emerging in a late time window, and source estimates pointing to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pisanu et al., 2024b)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that the influence of agreeableness on social information processing is not equally evident across all social and emotional processes but depends on the type and stage of processing considered.

Together, these findings provided the rationale for using the same three experimental tasks to investigate distinct social-cognitive processes previously examined in relation to agreeableness, as well as for using EEG to determine whether differences in the temporal dynamics of neural processing may emerge even when behavioral outcomes do not differ.
The three tasks range from the perception of social interactions to the recognition of basic emotional actions and the decoding of complex mental states.

The Social Interaction Task (SIT) requires participants to discriminate interacting from non-interacting individuals; the Biological (e)Motion task (BM) probes basic emotion recognition from dynamic pointlight body movements; and the Reading the Mind in the Eyes task (RME) requires the decoding of complex mental states from static eye-region information.

Together, these paradigms allowed us to examine whether the relationship between personality and social cognition extends across different social-cognitive processes or emerges selectively depending on the type of processing involved.
The present study extends our previous work to autistic adults without intellectual disability and with preserved language abilities.

Specifically, we asked whether personality, and agreeableness in particular, could account for part of the variability in the social and emotional processes previously investigated in neurotypical adults.
We addressed three research questions.

First, we investigated whether autistic participants showed a characteristic personality profile compared with a large neurotypical sample and, importantly, whether substantial interindividual variability was preserved within the autistic group.
Second, we asked whether autistic participants were more similar in agreeableness to neurotypical individuals with relatively low rather than high agreeableness.
Third, we investigated whether this pattern extended to behavioral performance and neural responses during the SIT, BM, and RME tasks.

Based on previous personality studies in autism (Lodi-Smith et al., 2019), we expected the autistic group to show lower mean scores on agreeableness, extraversion, conscientiousness, and openness, and higher neuroticism, while retaining substantial interindividual variability.
text.formatted: Based on previous personality studies in autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lodi-Smith et al., 2019)</ref>, we expected the autistic group to show lower mean scores on agreeableness, extraversion, conscientiousness, and openness, and higher neuroticism, while retaining substantial interindividual variability.

text.text: Given the lower agreeableness reported on average in autism, we further expected autistic participants to be closer to neurotypical participants with lower than with higher agreeableness scores.

We expected this relative proximity to be reflected, at least in part, in behavioral performance, although previous findings suggested that its expression might vary across social-cognitive processes.

At the neural level, our previous EEG studies provided more process-and time-specific predictions: agreeableness modulated neural responses during social interaction perception and, at a later processing stage, during complex mental-state decoding, but not during basic emotion recognition.

Accordingly, we expected group differences in neural activity to vary across tasks and processing stages, with a particularly clear difference between autistic and highly agreeable participants during the late stages of complex mental-state decoding.

Our previous studies showed that agreeableness is associated with some of the social-cognitive processes in neurotypical individuals.

In our previous work, higher agreeableness was associated with greater neural differentiation between social and non-social information during the perception of social interactions (Pisanu et al., 2024a), as well as with later neural activity during the decoding of complex mental states, whereas no comparable association emerged during the recognition of basic emotional actions (Pisanu et al., 2024b).

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that social-cognitive processing is modulated by individual differences in agreeableness, while also suggesting that this influence is not uniform but depends on the specific process involved and on the stage at which social information is processed.
More broadly, they highlight the importance of considering individual characteristics when investigating the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying social cognition.
This perspective may be particularly relevant to autism, given the substantial heterogeneity in social-cognitive functioning within the spectrum.

In the present study, we focused specifically on autistic young adults without intellectual or language impairment, a population in which individual differences in social-cognitive processing may be particularly important to characterize, and investigated whether individual differences in personality, with a particular focus on agreeableness, could contribute to characterizing social-cognitive processing.

To this aim, we used the same three experimental paradigms employed in our previous EEG studies (Pisanu et al., 2024a,b), allowing us to examine processes ranging from the perception of social interactions and basic emotional actions to the decoding of complex mental states.

text.text: In the following sections, we discuss the findings in relation to the three research questions outlined in the Introduction.
Regarding the first research question, we observed a personality profile tending towards lower scores in our autistic sample, in line with the meta-analysis by Lodi-Smith et al. (2019).

text.text: Autistic participants showed significantly lower scores in agreeableness, extraversion, conscientiousness, and higher neuroticism than a large neurotypical sample.
Contrary to our hypothesis, openness did not differ between groups.

One possible explanation is sample composition: our participants had no intellectual disability and preserved language abilities, whereas previous samples varied considerably in these characteristics (Lodi-Smith et al., 2019).

text.text: Importantly, relative to Italian normative values, autistic participants did not uniformly show extreme scores; rather, scores varied considerably within each trait, and only some individuals showed extreme values, as in the neurotypical sample.
These findings underscore the variability within this population, and argue against equating autism with a uniformly low personality profile.
They also suggest that personality assessment may help characterize individual strengths and difficulties, which could inform more tailored support.
Having the same diagnosis does not necessarily imply uniformity among individuals with that diagnosis.
Moving to the second research question, agreeableness showed the largest difference between the autistic and neurotypical groups.

As hypothesized, autistic participants showed agreeableness scores closer to those of neurotypical participants with lower agreeableness, while differentiating from those with higher agreeableness scores.

This result led us to pursue the third research question, asking whether the same pattern would also emerge across the social-cognitive processes investigated in our previous EEG studies (Pisanu et al., 2024a,b), at both the behavioral and neural levels.
text.formatted: This result led us to pursue the third research question, asking whether the same pattern would also emerge across the social-cognitive processes investigated in our previous EEG studies <ref type="bibr">(Pisanu et al., 2024a,b)</ref>, at both the behavioral and neural levels.

text.text: Our results indicated no significant behavioral group differences in the detection of social interaction and basic emotions, as measured by the SIT and BM tasks respectively.
However, significant differences emerged in the RME task.
Here, autistic participants exhibited lower accuracy in decoding complex mental states than HA participants, whereas no significant difference emerged relative to LA participants.

Thus, at the behavioral level, the pattern observed for agreeableness, a difference from HA but not from LA participants, was found during complex mentalstate decoding, but did not emerge as a generalized pattern across all the social-cognitive processes examined.
The neural results provided a more differentiated picture.
Consistent with the behavioral findings, no significant ERP differences emerged between groups in either the SIT or BM tasks.
In the RME task, however, two temporally and spatially distinct patterns were observed.
The first consisted of an early posterior effect, occurring approximately 120-170 ms after stimulus onset.

Effects with a highly consistent temporal and posterior distribution emerged in the emotion, age, and observe conditions in comparisons between the autistic group and the neurotypical groups, although the ASD-HA comparison did not reach significance in the age condition.
No corresponding difference emerged between HA and LA participants.

The timing and parieto-occipital distribution of this effect are consistent with the N170, a face-sensitive ERP component associated with the early perceptual processing of facial information (Feuerriegel et al., 2015; Kappenman et al., 2021; Rossion et al., 2003), which is typically reduced and/or delayed in ASD individuals (see Kang et al., 2018 for a meta-analysis).

text.text: A second pattern, specific to the mental-state decoding, emerged at later stages of processing and paralleled the behavioral results.
In the emotion condition, autistic participants showed a smaller positive amplitude over frontocentral sites than both neurotypical groups.
Significant clusters spanned approximately 450-1000 ms for the ASD-HA comparison and 400-600 ms for the ASD-LA comparison.

Importantly, no comparable late effect emerged in the age or observe conditions, suggesting this effect may be particularly relevant when participants are engaged in complex mental-state decoding, rather than reflecting a general response to visual stimuli.
This later effect is particularly interesting in relation to our previous EEG findings.
In neurotypical participants, agreeableness was associated with a late slow-wave response during complex mental-state decoding in the RME (Pisanu et al., 2024b).
text.formatted: In neurotypical participants, agreeableness was associated with a late slow-wave response during complex mental-state decoding in the RME <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pisanu et al., 2024b)</ref>.

text.text: The current late frontocentral effect partly overlaps with the temporal and spatial characteristics of this previous effect and is similarly selective for the condition requiring complex mental-state decoding.

Descriptively, and in line with our previous findings, HA participants exhibited the largest late positive activity, autistic participants the smallest, while LA participants tended to fall between the two.
This descriptive pattern should be interpreted cautiously, since no significant ERP differences emerged between HA and LA participants.

Nevertheless, the finding that autistic participants differed from both neurotypical groups indicates that the neural pattern cannot be reduced to a simple correspondence between autism and lower agreeableness.
This distinction becomes particularly relevant when behavioral and neural findings are considered together.
At the behavioral level, autistic participants differed from HA participants during mental-state decoding, whereas no significant difference was detected between autistic and LA participants.
At the neural level, however, autistic participants differed from both neurotypical groups.
Therefore, the behavioral similarity observed between autistic and LA participants did not correspond to a similar pattern of neural activity.
Agreeableness may contribute to characterizing individual variability in the absence of a significant behavioral difference between autistic and neurotypical participants.
More generally, these findings suggest that comparable behavioral outcomes do not necessarily imply similar temporal dynamics of the neural processes supporting those outcomes.

To sum up, the early posterior effect distinguished autistic from neurotypical participants regardless of agreeableness and experimental condition, whereas the late frontocentral effect was specific to mental-state decoding and paralleled the behavioral difference from HA participants.
One possible interpretation is that autistic and LA participants may achieve comparable behavioral outcomes through partly different processing dynamics.

In autistic individuals without intellectual and/or language impairment, such a dissociation could be compatible with the involvement of compensatory processes, whereby differences in neural processing do not necessarily result in corresponding differences in behavioral performance.
However, the present study does not directly demonstrate compensation or identify the strategies through which comparable performance may be achieved.

The current findings therefore provide evidence primarily for a dissociation between behavioral outcome and neural processing, while compensation remains one possible interpretation to be tested more directly in future studies.
Regarding the null results in the SIT and BM tasks, two considerations arise.
First, autistic individuals may experience difficulties in social interactions and emotional expression, yet this does not imply an inability to recognize such stimuli.
Difficulties in some of their social skills do not necessarily signify a comprehensive impairment in the realm of social cognition.
This is the rationale behind our approach of dissecting this domain, evaluating social and emotional aspects individually, while also accounting for task complexity.

This may be particularly true for autistic individuals without language and intellectual impairment who exhibit a certain degree of adaptability to environmental demands, including relational aspects (Kamp-Becker et al., 2010; Liss et al., 2001; Renty et al., 2006).
text.formatted: This may be particularly true for autistic individuals without language and intellectual impairment who exhibit a certain degree of adaptability to environmental demands, including relational aspects <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kamp-Becker et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Liss et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Renty et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: This finding is consistent with the idea that social-cognitive profiles in autism can be heterogeneous and that relatively preserved performance in some processes may coexist with differences in others.
Second, task characteristics should also be considered when interpreting the null findings.

As regards the recognition of basic emotions through point-light bodily stimuli (BM task), the extended duration and dynamic nature of these stimuli may provide participants with more information over time and therefore facilitate recognition.
It is possible that this additional processing time contributes to similar behavioral performance across groups, although the present design cannot establish this explanation.
Future studies manipulating stimulus duration or the amount of dynamic information available could test this possibility more directly.

Similarly, because the present EEG analyses of the BM focused on later processing stages, analyses specifically designed to characterize neural responses from stimulus onset could provide complementary information about earlier stages of biological-motion and emotion processing.
Notably, our tasks were not designed to emphasize response speed, which may explain the absence of group differences in reaction times.

Tasks requiring speeded responses could provide an interesting avenue to uncover distinctions, possibly not in terms of accuracy, but rather in terms of delayed responses among autistic participants, which could provide further evidence relevant to compensatory mechanisms.
Several limitations should be considered.
First, the autistic sample was relatively small, particularly for investigating interindividual variability, and replication in larger samples will be important.
Second, agreeableness is a continuous personality dimension, whereas the present study used HA and LA neurotypical groups to address the specific comparison with autistic participants.

Although this approach allowed us to test whether autistic participants more closely resembled neurotypical individuals differing in agreeableness, categorization inevitably reduces information about continuous individual variability.
This distinction is particularly important when comparing the present findings with our previous studies, in which agreeableness was examined as a continuous dimension.
Third, nonsignificant differences between groups cannot be interpreted as evidence of equivalence.

Finally, the three paradigms isolate specific components of social cognition under controlled experimental conditions and therefore cannot capture the full complexity of social functioning in everyday life.

Future studies using larger samples and combining dimensional personality measures with more naturalistic assessments of social cognition could further clarify how personality contributes to individual variability within autism.
Overall, these findings underscore the importance of considering individual variability within autism rather than relying on diagnostic status alone.

Recognizing individual strengths and difficulties may ultimately help inform more tailored interventions and support strategies aimed at promoting social participation and engagement in educational and occupational settings.
